description:
I’m Saloni Tangal, a product designer interested in human factors and designing for situations where help isn’t a tap away. For Space Apps, I’m exploring a question: what does it take to make a good decision when Earth can’t answer right away?

I’m participating solo this year and am here to meet others curious about design, health, and life in space.
summary:
Habitat Health is an interactive onboard tablet prototype that helps astronauts record health changes, compare them with their usual patterns, and privately request medical support during deep-space missions.

The prototype follows Maya Rao, a fictional astronaut who notices unexpected spotting during Mars transit while using menstrual suppression. Maya logs two observations, records uncertainty about her most recent dose, and compares what she noticed with her preflight baseline. She previews what the crew medical officer will receive and can send her crewmate a work-only update about their equipment inspection.

Habitat Health addresses the challenge through a complete workflow for gathering health indicators, assessing changes, and acting on them. It gives astronauts an onboard route to support when a reply from Earth is delayed, while helping them control what they share on a common crew device. The scenario is grounded in published spaceflight research and NASA guidance. Maya’s records and wearable readings are simulated.
details:
What I built

Habitat Health is a clickable prototype for a shared crew tablet. It connects preflight health setup, routine in-flight monitoring, private medical requests, the onboard medical officer’s workspace, and crewmate assistance. I focused on women astronauts to explore how a crew member could get help for a sensitive reproductive health concern while far from Earth.

How it works

Gather. Before launch, Maya and her flight surgeon establish a care profile with her usual pattern and medication context. In flight, Maya’s paired wearable supplies simulated readings (skin temperature, resting heart rate, breathing and sleep), shown beside her own usual range, and she can complete a routine check-in, and record changes she notices. In the walkthrough, she logs spotting at 08:10 and 11:40 and marks yesterday’s dose as “Not sure.”

Assess. Habitat Health compares her observations with her usual pattern. The timeline explicitly labels the gap “Not recorded between checks.” The interface distinguishes a missing observation, a detail Maya is unsure about, and information she chooses to keep private.

Act. Maya previews the information going to the onboard medical officer and can exclude optional medication or history details. The officer reviews the request in a private workspace and responds onboard. Maya can then send a work-only update about her 12:15 equipment inspection. The prototype also shows failed delivery, an alternate onboard contact route, and general help accessible from the locked tablet. If Maya cannot respond, a crewmate can alert the medical officer from the locked tablet with no sign-in and no access to private data. The officer sees Maya’s own log only if she chose that in her care profile.

Research and design decisions

NASA’s Five Hazards of Human Spaceflight, particularly distance from Earth, informed the decision to make the onboard medical officer the first point of contact in Maya’s walkthrough. NASA’s Ongoing Human Research Program Research informed the kinds of indicators considered for routine monitoring. NASA’s Risks of Human Spaceflight and the Canadian Space Agency’s overview of space experiments informed the broader scenario exploration.

Jain and Wotring’s 2016 paper on menstrual suppression in female astronauts and NASA’s 2026 human-spaceflight standard informed the choice of unexpected spotting during a mission. NASA’s medical care requirements provide additional context for abnormal uterine bleeding in mission planning. NASA’s Crew Interfaces guidance informed the use of written status labels alongside color, visible measurement units, and consistent controls. Iserson (2019) and Tissot et al. (2023) on remote and isolated care informed the crewmate and delayed-support scenarios.

Decision to source map

Onboard medical officer as the first contact: NASA’s Five Hazards of Human Spaceflight, distance from Earth. Routine indicators considered: NASA’s Ongoing HRP Research. Unexpected spotting as the scenario: Jain and Wotring (2016) and NASA-STD-3001 (2026). Abnormal uterine bleeding in mission planning: NASA-STD-3001 Appendix E. Written status labels with colour, visible units and consistent controls: NASA-STD-3001 Section 10, Crew Interfaces. Crewmate help from a locked tablet and delayed-support scenarios: Iserson (2019) and Tissot et al. (2023).

How I checked the design

The interface follows measurable legibility rules from my design system: pure black text at 20:1 contrast, status and action colours at 6.6:1 or better, a 14 px minimum text size, and 48 px touch targets. Status colours are always paired with written labels. These are design checks, not clinical validation.

Why this matters beyond one scenario

Maya’s case is one example of a wider problem: getting private, trustworthy help on a shared device when a reply from Earth is delayed. The same pattern, an onboard-first route to care, controlled sharing, and help from a crewmate who isn’t medically trained, applies to other sensitive conditions and to other isolated settings, such as polar stations and remote clinics. The sources I drew on for remote and isolated care (Iserson 2019; Tissot et al. 2023) come from these settings. Habitat Health starts with menstrual and reproductive health, where private care is often overlooked. The same private, observation-first workflow could support other sex-specific concerns, such as urinary and reproductive health for crew with male physiology, as well as concerns that apply to everyone, like sleep, dizziness and sudden difficulty with a task. I listed 50 circumstances that could challenge the same workflow, from routine checks to emergencies where a crewmate takes over, and the full list is in the FigJam. Any use would need its own approved clinical protocols.

What makes it different and what I would test next

The same tablet supports three interactions in Maya’s scenario. She can interpret a change privately, hand over relevant information to the officer, and coordinate work with her crewmate using a separate message. Designing all three together made it possible to show exactly who sees what.

In a future simulated crew exercise, I would measure time to reach onboard help, whether astronauts can correctly identify what they will share, and whether they can recover after failed delivery. I would also replay a year of simulated health histories across preflight, transit, and a Mars surface stay to test how the workflow handles different crew profiles and incomplete records. NASA’s CHAPEA Mission 2 provides a precedent for a long-duration Mars-habitat exercise.

Limits. Habitat Health is a design prototype. It makes no diagnosis, uses no real crew data, and gives no validated medical advice. Operational use would need approved clinical protocols, authentication, encryption, secure communications and usability evaluation with astronauts. NASA sources inform the context and design decisions, but they do not validate the prototype.

Tools, data, and Super Intelligence disclosure

Tools and data. I used FigJam to explore scenarios, map user flows, and refine the wireframes through a heuristic review. During early development, I experimented with Bolt and Lovable, explored Supabase for the backend, and used Visual Studio Code. Within the hackathon timeframe, I completed the interactive walkthrough in Claude Design and submitted it as the Habitat Health prototype. Maya’s health profile, observations, and wearable readings are simulated.

Super Intelligence (SI) disclosure. The concept, research, scenario and design decisions in Habitat Health are mine. I used Bolt and Lovable for early implementation experiments. I used Claude Design to build the interactive prototype, the demo slides and the project page. Google Gemini and ChatGPT helped with wireframe exploration and submission copy. All crew data, including Maya’s profile, observations and wearable readings, is fictional and simulated.
